paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie were sitting on the porch of their house.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie are at home, outside their house.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie sat outside the front door of their house. Annie looked down the street at the woods. Jack read a book.

background.note: Frog Creek is the small town in Pennsylvania, USA, where Jack and Annie live. The magic tree house is in the Frog Creek woods.

paragraphs.context: He saw a rabbit with very long legs
paragraphs.mainIdea: A strange rabbit hops into the woods.
paragraphs.simple: Jack saw a rabbit with very long legs. It jumped down their street, left the path and went into the woods.

paragraphs.context: "He's a sign," said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie thinks the rabbit is telling them something.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the rabbit is a sign: it shows them that something will happen.

paragraphs.context: "Don't worry," said Annie. "You know when we leave in the tree house, time stops."
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says they will not be late for dinner.
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells Jack not to worry. When they travel in the tree house, time at home stops. So they will be back before dinner.

paragraphs.context: Jack pulled on his backpack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack tells his parents he is going out.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put on his backpack. He shouted through the door: "I will be back in ten minutes!" Then he went after Annie.

background.note: Many American houses have a screen door: a light door made of thin wire net, outside the main door. It lets air in and keeps insects out.

paragraphs.context: The rabbit was standing in a ray of sunlight.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The rabbit runs off when it sees them.
paragraphs.simple: The rabbit stood in a line of sunlight. When it saw Jack and Annie, it ran away fast.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie waved back to her. As always
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is very happy to see Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie waved to Morgan. Jack always feels very happy when he sees the magic librarian.

background.note: Morgan le Fay is an enchantress (a woman who can do magic) and a librarian. In these books she collects books from all through time.

paragraphs.context: "Perhaps," said Morgan. She smiled mysteriously.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan does not say clearly if the rabbit is her friend.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan only says "Perhaps" and smiles in a strange, secret way. She says she has many strange friends. Annie jokes that she and Jack are some of them.
paragraphs.tone: A small joke: Annie says that she and Jack are Morgan's "odd" (strange) friends too.

paragraphs.context: "I'm still having problems with Merlin,"
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan is busy, so Jack and Annie will help her.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says she still has trouble with Merlin, so she has little time for her real work. But soon Jack and Annie will become Master Librarians, and that will help her a lot.

background.note: In the series, Jack and Annie must solve four riddles. Then they become Master Librarians, who can travel through time to collect books.
Merlin is a famous magician from old British stories about King Arthur.

paragraphs.context: Jack smiled. He was going to be a Master Librarian
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack can hardly believe his good luck.
paragraphs.simple: Jack smiled. Soon he would be a Master Librarian who travels through time and space. It seemed almost too good to be true.

paragraphs.context: The title of the book was Days of the Wild West.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan gives them a book about the Wild West.
paragraphs.simple: The book is called "Days of the Wild West". Its cover shows a town in the American West, on a big, flat grassy land.

background.note: The "Wild West" is the western part of America in the 1800s, when new towns, cowboys and horses spread across the land. Life there was hard and often dangerous.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath. Just how wild?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is a little afraid of the Wild West.
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathed in deeply. He asked himself: how wild (how dangerous) will this place be?
paragraphs.tone: Jack plays with the word "wild". He is nervous, but it is also a little funny.

paragraphs.context: Morgan reached into the folds of her robe again
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan gives Annie the riddle.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan put her hand into her long robe again and took out a rolled paper. She gave it to Annie.

paragraphs.context: "Yes," said Morgan. "Then you'll only have two more to solve.
paragraphs.mainIdea: After this riddle there will be only two more.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says this is the riddle. After they solve it, they will only have two more riddles to solve.

paragraphs.context: The tree house had landed in a lone tree on a prairie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house lands on the prairie.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is now in one tree, all alone, on a big flat grassland. It is late in the day.

background.note: A prairie is a huge, flat land covered with grass, in the middle of North America. There are very few trees.

paragraphs.context: Right in front of them was the town from the cover of the book.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The town looks empty and frightening.
paragraphs.simple: The town from the book cover is just in front of them. But in real life it looks empty and a little frightening.

paragraphs.context: To one side of the town was a patch of ground with several tombstones.
paragraphs.mainIdea: There is a small graveyard near the town.
paragraphs.simple: Next to the town is a small area with some grave stones, where dead people are buried.

paragraphs.context: Out of the blue,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The riddle begins.
paragraphs.simple: The riddle says: Suddenly, my lonely voice calls out to you. Who am I? Am I?
paragraphs.tone: A riddle poem. "Out of the blue" means suddenly, when you do not expect it. Think about why "Am I?" comes twice.

paragraphs.context: There were no human sounds at all
paragraphs.mainIdea: The place is very quiet.
paragraphs.simple: They cannot hear any people. They only hear flies and the dry wind.

paragraphs.context: In the 1870s, Rattlesnake Flats was a rest stop
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains the town's history.
paragraphs.simple: In the 1870s, this town was a place where the stagecoach stopped for a rest. The stagecoach carried people from Santa Fe in New Mexico to Fort Worth in Texas.

background.note: A stagecoach was a big carriage pulled by four or six horses. Before trains, it carried people and letters across the West. It stopped at "stages" (rest stops) to change horses.
Santa Fe is an old city in New Mexico, in the south-west of the USA.
Fort Worth is a city in Texas. It was a famous cowboy town.

paragraphs.context: When the creek dried up, everyone left.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The town became a ghost town.
paragraphs.simple: When the small river had no more water, all the people left. By 1880 no one lived there. It was a "ghost town".

background.note: A ghost town is a town where nobody lives any more. Many towns in the American West were left empty when the water, gold or work was gone.

background.note: A tumbleweed is a dry plant that breaks off at the root. The wind rolls it along the ground. In films, tumbleweeds show an empty, lonely western town.

paragraphs.context: "There!" Annie pointed to a rattlesnake.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie sees a rattlesnake.
paragraphs.simple: Annie points to a rattlesnake about 30 metres away. It is lying in rings and shaking its tail to make a noise.

background.note: A rattlesnake is a poisonous snake in America. The end of its tail has dry rings that make a shaking sound. It rattles to say "Stay away!"

paragraphs.context: "I guess that's why this town is called Rattlesnake Flats,"
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie understands the name of the town.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the town is named after the rattlesnakes. ("Flats" means flat land.)
paragraphs.tone: A small joke: now Annie knows why the town has this name.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked around. The town was hardly big enough to call a town.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The town is very small.
paragraphs.simple: The town was so small that it was almost not a town. It had one dirt street and a few old buildings.

paragraphs.context: She pointed to a building. The faded sign said GENERAL STORE.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They find an old shop.
paragraphs.simple: Annie points to a building with an old sign: GENERAL STORE. She wants to look inside for the answer to the riddle.

background.note: A general store was a shop in a small town in the Old West. It sold almost everything: food, clothes, tools and animal food.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie stepped onto the porch. The wooden boards creaked loudly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The store is old and dirty.
paragraphs.simple: The wood on the floor made loud noises when they walked on it. The door had fallen off. Inside, the air was full of dust, and there were spider webs on the ceiling.

paragraphs.context: "Careful," said Jack. He poked at other stuff in the store
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack looks at the old things in the store.
paragraphs.simple: Jack touched other old things: a bag for animal food, a cup made of old metal, and a calendar from 1878.

paragraphs.context: "Oh, wow," said Annie. She held up two cowboy hats.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie finds cowboy hats.
paragraphs.simple: Annie finds two cowboy hats. She puts one on and gives the other one to Jack.

background.note: A cowboy hat has a wide brim (edge) all around. It keeps the hot sun and rain off a rider's face.

paragraphs.context: Jack blew on his hat. A cloud of dust rose up.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The hat is very dusty.
paragraphs.simple: Jack blew on the hat. A lot of dust came out, and he sneezed.

paragraphs.context: "Boots!" said Annie. She pointed to a row of cowboy boots on a shelf.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie finds cowboy boots for them.
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees cowboy boots on a shelf. Some are small, the right size for them. She gives a pair to Jack.

background.note: Cowboy boots are tall leather boots with a pointed front and a heel. They help a rider keep his feet in the stirrups.

paragraphs.context: "I know, but just try them on," said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack checks the boots before he puts them on.
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells Jack to put them on. Jack turns his boots over and shakes them hard.

paragraphs.context: "Checking for scorpions," Jack said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is afraid there may be scorpions in the boots.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says he is looking for scorpions.
paragraphs.tone: Jack is careful, as always. Annie laughs at him.

background.note: Scorpions are small animals with a poisonous tail. They live in hot, dry places and sometimes hide in shoes.

paragraphs.context: Jack sighed. He pulled off his sneakers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boots are too hard and they hurt.
paragraphs.simple: Jack took off his sports shoes and pushed his feet into the boots. The boots were very hard. When he tried to walk, they hurt.

paragraphs.context: Jack threw his sneakers into his backpack and hobbled after Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack follows Annie slowly.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put his sports shoes in his bag. He walked after Annie slowly, because the boots hurt his feet.

paragraphs.context: She crept toward a building that had a sign with the word HOTEL on it.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They go quietly toward the hotel.
paragraphs.simple: Annie moved quietly toward a building with a HOTEL sign. Jack walked after her, but he could not walk well in the boots.

paragraphs.context: The fading daylight lit a piano
paragraphs.mainIdea: A piano is playing, but nobody is there.
paragraphs.simple: The last light of the day showed a piano in the corner. The keys were going up and down. But no one was playing it!

paragraphs.context: Suddenly the keys were still. The air got very cold.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The piano stops and the room gets cold.
paragraphs.simple: The piano keys stopped moving. Suddenly the air was very cold.
paragraphs.tone: This is the scary part. A cold room is a sign of a ghost in many ghost stories.

paragraphs.context: "Yeah, but that was ancient Egypt," said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not want to believe in ghosts.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they saw a ghost in ancient Egypt, but this is different. He says he does not believe it, but his heart is beating very fast.

background.note: In book 2 (Mummies in the Morning), Jack and Annie went to ancient Egypt and met the ghost of a queen.

paragraphs.context: Player pianos were popular in the Old West.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains how a player piano works.
paragraphs.simple: Many people in the Old West had pianos that play by themselves. Someone pushed the floor pedals with their feet. Later, pianos used electricity to play all alone.

background.note: A player piano plays music by itself. A roll of paper with holes tells it which keys to press. At first, a person pushed pedals with their feet to make it work.

paragraphs.context: "Whew." Jack closed the book.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks there must be electricity.
paragraphs.simple: Jack feels better. He thinks the piano is an electric one that started by itself.

paragraphs.context: "I didn't know they had electricity in the Wild West,"
paragraphs.mainIdea: There was no electricity, so it may be a ghost.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks: did they have electricity in the Wild West? Jack says no. Then he understands: no one is playing the piano, so it could be a ghost!
paragraphs.tone: Funny and scary: Jack's "clever" answer is wrong, and he is suddenly afraid.

paragraphs.context: A cloud of dust seemed to be moving toward the town.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Riders are coming to the town.
paragraphs.simple: A cloud of dust came toward the town. Then Jack saw three men on horses. They were moving a small group of horses.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie hurried to the empty barrels.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They hide in barrels.
paragraphs.simple: They ran to the empty barrels. Jack got into one, but his hat did not fit. He jumped out, threw his hat into the hotel, and got back in just in time.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard the horses thunder into town.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The cowboys ride into town.
paragraphs.simple: The horses ran into the town with a loud noise. Through a small hole in the barrel Jack saw cowboys and horses go past very fast.

paragraphs.context: "The creek bed must have dried up!" a cowboy yelled.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The cowboys see that the town is empty.
paragraphs.simple: A cowboy shouts that the river has no water, so the town is empty, like a ghost.

paragraphs.context: Jack really had to sneeze now.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack cannot stop a sneeze.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to sneeze. He presses his nose hard. But he cannot stop it, and he makes a small "Ah-choo!" sound.
paragraphs.tone: Funny but scary: a sneeze could show the cowboys where Jack is hiding.

paragraphs.context: Just then a loud whinny split the air.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A wild horse fights the cowboys.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly a horse made a loud cry. Jack saw a beautiful horse stand up on her back legs.

paragraphs.context: She had no rider or saddle, just a rope around her neck.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack describes the beautiful red horse.
paragraphs.simple: The horse had no rider and no seat on her back, only a rope on her neck. She was red like the evening sky, with a black mane and a white star on her head.

paragraphs.context: "He was too slow," a growly voice said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The men will sell the mare far away.
paragraphs.simple: The men left the baby horse behind because he was too slow. A man with a low, rough voice says they will sell the mare in another country.

background.note: The "border" here is the line between the USA and Mexico. The men want to sell the stolen horse far away, where no one will know.

paragraphs.context: That's terrible! thought Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is worried about Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks it is very bad. He knows Annie is unhappy too. He hopes she will not jump out of her barrel.

paragraphs.context: "I know. But there was nothing we could do," said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack says they could not help, and his boots hurt.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they could not do anything. His boots hurt him a lot. He climbs out of the barrel.
hardWords: there was nothing we could do
paragraphs.tone: "His boots were killing him" is a funny way to say the boots hurt very much.

paragraphs.context: A small horse was running down the road.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The baby horse comes into town.
paragraphs.simple: A small horse ran down the road. He was red like his mother, with the same black mane and white star. He had a rope on his neck and looked lost.

paragraphs.context: At the end of the 1800s, over a million wild horses
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains mustangs.
paragraphs.simple: In the late 1800s, more than a million wild horses called mustangs lived in the West. They came from Spanish horses that had run away. Men caught them and sold them to farmers. It was very hard to train a wild mustang.

background.note: Mustangs are wild horses of the American West. Their families came from horses that Spanish people brought to America about 500 years ago.
A rancher owns a ranch: a very large farm in the American West with cows or horses.

paragraphs.context: She slowly reached out and grabbed the end of his rope.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie leads the colt to a post.
paragraphs.simple: Annie slowly took the end of the colt's rope. She kept talking to him and led him to a wide wooden pole.

paragraphs.context: The basic rules on how to treat a horse are simple
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book gives rules for horses.
paragraphs.simple: The rules are easy: touch the horse gently, speak in a strong and sure voice, be happy, say "good horse", and give him something nice.

paragraphs.context: But Annie was already sitting on the colt's back!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie is already riding the colt.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wanted to tell Annie the rules, but she was already on the horse's back!
paragraphs.tone: Funny: Jack reads the rules, but Annie does it all before he finishes.

paragraphs.context: Annie kept patting his neck and talking softly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The colt becomes calm.
paragraphs.simple: Annie kept touching his neck gently and talking quietly. In the end, the young horse stopped moving.

paragraphs.context: "Are you nuts?" said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not want to follow the bad men.
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks if Annie is crazy. They must solve the riddle, and it will soon be dark. He could see that those men were very bad.

paragraphs.context: Wild mustangs live together in families.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says a young mustang needs its mother.
paragraphs.simple: Wild horses live in families. A mother and her baby love each other very much. When the baby makes sad or hungry sounds, the mother always comes. A mustang cannot live happily alone.

paragraphs.context: He huffed and puffed and pulled.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A man with a gun stops them.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pulled hard at his boot, breathing loudly. Then a low voice shouted: "Put your hands up, or I will shoot!" Jack stopped at once.

paragraphs.context: A cowboy rode out of an alley.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A cowboy with a gun comes out.
paragraphs.simple: A cowboy came out of a narrow street on a gray horse. His face was thin and brown from the sun. He had a gun in his hand.

background.note: A six-shooter is a small gun that holds six bullets. It is also called a revolver. Many cowboys carried one.

paragraphs.context: "I reckon you're the smallest horse thieves
paragraphs.mainIdea: The cowboy thinks they are stealing his horse.
paragraphs.simple: The cowboy says: "I think you are the smallest horse thieves I have ever met."
paragraphs.tone: The cowboy is joking a little, because they are only children.

background.note: In the Old West, a horse was very important and cost a lot. Stealing a horse was a very serious crime.

paragraphs.context: "Yup, must be the rustlers that stole my last five mustangs,"
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bad men stole horses from this cowboy too.
paragraphs.simple: The cowboy says the bad men must be the thieves who took his five horses.

background.note: Rustlers were thieves who stole cows or horses in the Old West.

paragraphs.context: The cowboy put away his six-shooter.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The cowboy is friendly now.
paragraphs.simple: The cowboy puts his gun away. He says Annie is brave and gives her a funny name: Smiley.

paragraphs.context: "Every cowpoke's got to have a nickname,"
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cowboys give everyone a nickname.
paragraphs.simple: The cowboy says every cowboy must have a special friendly name.

background.note: A nickname is a friendly name that is not your real name. Slim calls Annie "Smiley" because she smiles a lot, and Jack "Shorty" because he is short.

paragraphs.context: Jack agreed. Slim was slim. And Dusty was dusty.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The names fit the cowboy and his horse.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks the names are right: the cowboy is thin, and his horse is covered with dust.
paragraphs.tone: A word joke: "Slim" is a name, and "slim" also means thin. "Dusty" is a name, and "dusty" means covered with dust.

paragraphs.context: "Um . . . the stagecoach," said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie makes up a story.
paragraphs.simple: Annie cannot say they came by magic. So she says they came on the stagecoach and asked the driver to let them get out here.

paragraphs.context: Slim looked around. "I'll say," he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim agrees it was a mistake.
paragraphs.simple: Slim says "I'll say!", which means "Yes, that is very true!" Annie says they will leave when the next stagecoach comes.

paragraphs.context: "Hmm, must be over yonder," said Slim.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim looks at the hill where the rustlers are.
paragraphs.simple: Slim says the rustlers must be over there. He looks at a low hill far away. The sun looks like a red ball above it.

paragraphs.context: "No, we have to stay here," Jack said quickly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to stay and solve the riddle.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they must stay. Slim can help the colt now, so Jack wants to look for the answer to the riddle. And he still wants to take off his boots.

paragraphs.context: For starters, he wanted Slim to stop
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants Slim to think he is brave.
paragraphs.simple: First, Jack wants Slim to stop calling him Shorty. And he wants Slim to think he is brave. So he says he wants to go too.
paragraphs.tone: Jack is not really brave here. He just does not want to look scared. It is a little funny.

paragraphs.context: "I wouldn't say 'yes' to many kids, Smiley
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim lets Annie ride the colt.
paragraphs.simple: Slim does not say yes to many children, but Annie is good with horses. He tells her to hold the mane tightly. He will pull the colt behind him.

paragraphs.context: Jack bounced up and down. His boots hurt.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ride is hard for Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack goes up and down on the horse. His boots hurt and the sun is in his eyes.

paragraphs.context: "Hear that?" said Slim. "The mare.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mare knows her colt is near.
paragraphs.simple: Slim says the mother horse feels that her baby is near, so she is crying out.

paragraphs.context: "Once the mare's loose, she'll break for Sunset,"
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim explains his plan.
paragraphs.simple: When the mother horse is free, she will run fast to her baby. Then Annie and the colt must ride away fast.

paragraphs.context: "Then we'll split the wind," said Slim.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim uses cowboy words Jack does not know.
paragraphs.simple: Slim says they will "split the wind" (ride very fast) until they get to Blue Canyon. Jack does not understand, but he does not ask.
paragraphs.tone: Funny: Jack asks every question only in his head. Annie has no questions at all.

paragraphs.context: Fun? thought Jack. Is she nuts? Our lives are at stake.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks it is dangerous, not fun.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says "Have fun", but Jack thinks she is crazy. They could die!

paragraphs.context: Slim snapped his reins. Dusty started down the rise.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They ride down the hill at night.
paragraphs.simple: Slim shook the reins and the horse went down the small hill. The moon and many stars gave them light.

paragraphs.context: "Whoa!" he said firmly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack uses the horse rules, and they work.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says "Whoa!" in a strong voice. To his surprise, Dusty stops and is quiet. Then Jack uses another rule: be happy. He tells Dusty everything will be fine.

paragraphs.context: Instead, Slim rode right past him!
paragraphs.mainIdea: The horses run away after the colt.
paragraphs.simple: Slim rode past Jack. Annie rode away on the colt. The mother horse ran after her baby, and all the other mustangs ran after the mother.

paragraphs.context: Dusty cleared the rise in an awkward leap.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack falls off the horse.
paragraphs.simple: Dusty jumped over the top of the hill in a bad way. Jack started to fall. He let go of the reins and tried to hold the saddle, but he was too heavy, and he fell to the ground.

background.note: The saddle horn is the high part at the front of a cowboy saddle. A rider can hold it, or tie a rope to it.

paragraphs.context: A shimmering white figure was moving across the top of the rise!
paragraphs.mainIdea: A ghost frightens the rustlers' horses.
paragraphs.simple: A shining white shape moved across the top of the hill. The rustlers' horses were very afraid and moved back.

paragraphs.context: Jack didn't have time to think about what he was seeing.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack gets away.
paragraphs.simple: Jack did not stop to think. He knew this was his only chance to get away. He used all his power to get back on the horse.

paragraphs.context: Slim steered the herd to the left.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They take the horses to Blue Canyon.
paragraphs.simple: Slim moved the horses to the left. He took them through a deep, narrow way between rocks. Then they came to an open space with rock walls all around, in the moonlight.

paragraphs.context: "We'll corral the mustangs here in Blue Canyon,"
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim keeps the horses in the canyon.
paragraphs.simple: Slim says they will keep the horses here, because the rock walls are like a fence.

background.note: A corral is a fenced place where cowboys keep horses or cows. Here the canyon walls work like a fence.

paragraphs.context: As Jack patted Dusty's damp neck
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thanks Dusty.
paragraphs.simple: Jack touched Dusty's wet neck and remembered the last rules: say "good horse" and give a reward. So he thanked Dusty and said he was great.

paragraphs.context: As Jack carried the saddlebags
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is very tired but happy.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's boots felt hard and tight. His legs hurt and were weak. But he did not care.

paragraphs.context: "Do you know the answer to this riddle?" Jack asked.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack asks Slim about the riddle.
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks Slim if he knows the answer to the riddle. He says the whole riddle again.

paragraphs.context: "It's Lonesome Luke," said Slim.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim says a cowboy ghost plays the piano.
paragraphs.simple: Slim says the piano player is the ghost of a cowboy called Lonesome Luke. Jack sits up quickly.

paragraphs.context: "I saw him! I saw him!" he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack understands the ghost helped him.
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers the white shape on the hill. It was the ghost! It frightened the rustlers. Without it, Jack could not have got away.

paragraphs.context: "Years ago, Lonesome Luke had a gal
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim tells the ghost story.
paragraphs.simple: Long ago, Luke loved a young woman very much. But life in the Wild West was too hard for her, so she went back to the east of America.

paragraphs.context: "Luke went loco. Every night he'd show up at the hotel
paragraphs.mainIdea: Luke became crazy and died.
paragraphs.simple: Luke became crazy with sadness. Every night he played the same song on the hotel piano. One night he went into the prairie and never came back.

background.note: "Red River Valley" is an old American cowboy song. It is a sad love song about someone who is leaving.

paragraphs.context: Slim took out a harmonica.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim plays the ghost's song.
paragraphs.simple: Slim played a song on a small music instrument. It was the same sad song they heard in the hotel.

background.note: A harmonica is a small music instrument that you blow into. Cowboys often carried one and played it by the fire.

paragraphs.context: Jack lay back down and listened to the lonesome tune.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack falls asleep.
paragraphs.simple: Jack lay down and listened to the sad song. A wild animal cried far away. The horses moved in the dark.

background.note: A coyote is a wild animal like a small wolf. It lives in North America and howls at night.

paragraphs.context: "A cowboy always carries biscuits and a canteen of coffee,"
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cowboy breakfast.
paragraphs.simple: Slim says a cowboy always has bread and a bottle of coffee with him.

background.note: In America, a biscuit is a small round bread, not a sweet cookie.
A canteen is a small bottle for water or another drink, often made of metal.

paragraphs.context: "It's hard as a rock," Slim said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The food is not good, but cowboys don't mind.
paragraphs.simple: Slim says the biscuit is very hard and the coffee tastes bad, like dirty river water. But a cowboy eats what he can get.

paragraphs.context: "Head south with my herd," said Slim.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim tells his plans.
paragraphs.simple: Slim will go south with his horses and sell them. Then he will ride across the flat lands and catch more wild horses.

paragraphs.context: "He likes writing things clown," said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says Jack likes to write notes.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says Jack likes writing things down. ("clown" is a mistake in the printed book. It should be "down".)

paragraphs.context: "Oh, yeah?" said Slim. "Me too.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim wanted to be a writer.
paragraphs.simple: Slim says he also likes to write. He first came to the West to write a book. But many things happened, and now he catches and sells wild horses.

paragraphs.context: Slim kept staring at his herd.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim decides to be a writer.
paragraphs.simple: Slim looked at his horses for a long time. He says he could live in Laramie and write. Then he would not need to run after horse thieves.

background.note: Laramie is a town in Wyoming, in the American West.

paragraphs.context: Out of the blue, a voice called, "Bye!"
paragraphs.mainIdea: Someone answers Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly a voice said "Bye!" Annie is surprised. She thinks it is the ghost.

paragraphs.context: "Nope," said Jack. "It's just an echo.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack explains the voice.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says it is an echo: the sound hits the canyon walls and comes back.

background.note: An echo happens when a sound hits a hard wall, like rock, and comes back to you. You can hear your own voice again.

paragraphs.context: "You know, Shorty," he said, "you might be short
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim says Jack is very clever.
paragraphs.simple: Slim says Jack is short, but very tall in his brains: he is very clever.
paragraphs.tone: A friendly joke. Slim plays with "short" and "tall" to praise Jack.

paragraphs.context: "And, Smiley," Slim said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim says Annie is very brave.
paragraphs.simple: Slim says Annie's great courage is "nothing to smile about".
paragraphs.tone: A play on words. "Nothing to smile about" usually means something bad. Slim means her courage is serious and important, and he plays with her name "Smiley".

paragraphs.context: "I'm grateful to you both for steering me straight,"
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim thanks them for helping him.
paragraphs.simple: Slim thanks them for helping him choose the right way in life. He promises to thank them one day.

paragraphs.context: Slim Cooley turned one last time.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim says goodbye and rides away.
paragraphs.simple: Slim turned one more time and waved his hat. He said goodbye and rode off toward the setting sun.
paragraphs.tone: "Rode off into the sunset" is how many old cowboy films end.

paragraphs.context: The piano was playing "Red River Valley."
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see the ghost at the piano.
paragraphs.simple: The piano played the sad song. On the piano seat they saw the shining shape of a cowboy, but they could not see him well.

paragraphs.context: Then the ghost of Lonesome Luke faded away.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ghost goes away.
paragraphs.simple: The ghost slowly went away. Cold air moved past them, and they both shook.

paragraphs.context: Annie still held the ancient scroll.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie puts the scroll with the other one.
paragraphs.simple: Annie still had the old scroll. She put it in the corner next to the scroll from the ocean trip (book 9).

paragraphs.context: The author's name was below the title.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim wrote the book!
paragraphs.simple: The writer's name was under the title in small letters: Slim Cooley. Slim wrote the book they used!

paragraphs.context: Jack opened Slim's book. He looked at the title page.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book was made in 1895.
paragraphs.simple: At the bottom of the first page Jack read where and when the book was made: Texas Press, Dallas, 1895.

background.note: This tells the name of the company that made the book (Texas Press), the city (Dallas, in Texas) and the year (1895).

paragraphs.context: WITH THANKS TO SMILEY AND SHORTY
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim thanks Jack and Annie in his book.
paragraphs.simple: Slim wrote at the front of the book: Thank you to Smiley and Shorty, two people I did not know, who changed my life.
paragraphs.tone: A happy and touching ending. Slim kept his promise to thank them.

paragraphs.context: "I know," said Jack. "But when we read his book
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slim's book is like an echo.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says that reading Slim's book is like hearing him talk. Annie says it is like an echo from the past.
paragraphs.tone: The story ends with the riddle word "echo" used in a new way: a book lets a voice from long ago come back to us.

sentences.context: "I'm still having problems with Merlin," said the enchantress, "which leaves me little time to do my real work.
sentences.simple: Morgan said: "I still have trouble with Merlin, so I do not have much time for my real work."
sentences.main: I'm having problems, which leaves me little time.

Morgan said,
and this gives me only a little time
to do my real job.

sentences.grammar: "Said the enchantress" breaks Morgan's words into two parts. "Which" points back to the problems with Merlin. "Little time" means not much time.

sentences.context: But soon you both will become Master Librarians, and that will be a big help to me."
sentences.simple: But soon you two will be Master Librarians, and that will help me a lot.
sentences.main: You will become Master Librarians.

parts.meaning: But soon you two will be Master Librarians,

parts.text: and that will be a big help to me."
parts.meaning: and this will help me very much.

sentences.grammar: "That" means "you becoming Master Librarians".

sentences.context: He was going to be a Master Librarian who traveled through time and space.
sentences.simple: Soon he would be a Master Librarian. He would travel through time and space.
sentences.main: He was going to be a Master Librarian.

sentences.context: There were no human sounds at all—only the buzzing of flies and the whistling of the dry wind.
sentences.simple: They could hear no people. They could only hear flies and the wind.
sentences.main: There were no human sounds.

sentences.context: In the 1870s, Rattlesnake Flats was a rest stop for the stagecoach that carried passengers from Santa Fe, New Mexico, to Fort Worth, Texas.
sentences.simple: In the 1870s the stagecoach stopped at this town. The stagecoach took people from Santa Fe to Fort Worth.
sentences.main: Rattlesnake Flats was a rest stop.

parts.meaning: Between 1870 and 1879,

parts.text: Rattlesnake Flats was a rest stop
parts.meaning: this town was a place to stop and rest
for the big horse carriage
which took people
from the city of Santa Fe in New Mexico
to the city of Fort Worth in Texas.

sentences.grammar: Read "City, State": "Santa Fe, New Mexico" is a city and the state it is in. "That carried ..." tells you about the stagecoach.

sentences.context: He poked at other stuff in the store—an old feed sack, a rusted tin cup, a faded calendar dated 1878.
sentences.simple: He touched other old things in the shop: a bag for animal food, an old metal cup, and a calendar from 1878.
sentences.main: He poked at other stuff.

parts.text: He poked at other stuff in the store
parts.meaning: He touched other things in the shop
an old bag for animal food,
an old metal cup with red-brown rust,
an old calendar for the year 1878.

sentences.grammar: After the dash comes a list of the "stuff". Each thing is cut off by a comma.

sentences.context: The piano played automatically when someone pumped its floor pedals.
sentences.simple: The piano played by itself when a person pushed the pedals with their feet.
sentences.main: The piano played automatically.

parts.meaning: The piano played by itself

parts.text: when someone pumped its floor pedals.
parts.meaning: when a person pushed the foot parts up and down.

sentences.grammar: "When ..." tells you what made the piano play.

sentences.context: When they got outside, they heard another sound: horse hooves thumping against the hard ground.
sentences.simple: Outside, they heard a new sound: horses' feet hitting the hard ground.
sentences.main: They heard another sound.

parts.meaning: When they came out,
they heard a new sound:

parts.text: horse hooves thumping against the hard ground.
parts.meaning: horses' feet hitting the hard ground with a low noise.

sentences.grammar: The colon (:) means "here is what it was".

sentences.context: The ground rang from the pounding of hooves as they galloped off.
sentences.simple: The ground made a loud noise from the horses' feet as they ran away fast.
sentences.main: The ground rang.

parts.meaning: The ground was full of loud noise
because the horses' feet hit it hard
while they ran away very fast.

sentences.grammar: "Rang" is the past of "ring" (make a loud sound). "As" here means "while".

sentences.context: These tough, fast horses were descendants of runaway Spanish horses.
sentences.simple: These strong, fast horses came from Spanish horses that had run away.
sentences.main: These horses were descendants.

parts.meaning: These strong and fast horses
were the great-great-grandchildren
of horses that ran away from Spanish people.

sentences.grammar: "Descendants of" = the children and grandchildren of. "Runaway" tells you the Spanish horses ran away.

sentences.context: The basic rules on how to treat a horse are simple: a soft hand, a firm voice, a sunny attitude, praise, and reward.
sentences.simple: Here are the easy rules for a horse: touch it gently, speak strongly, be happy, say nice things, and give it something good.
sentences.main: The rules are simple.

parts.text: The basic rules on how to treat a horse
parts.meaning: The main rules for how to be with a horse
are easy:
touch it gently,
speak in a strong, sure voice,
be happy and cheerful,
say "good horse",
and give it something nice.

sentences.grammar: After the colon (:) comes a list of five rules.

sentences.context: His sounds of distress or hunger will always bring her to him.
sentences.simple: When the young horse makes sad or hungry sounds, his mother always comes to him.
sentences.main: His sounds will bring her to him.

parts.text: His sounds of distress or hunger
parts.meaning: When the young horse cries because he is afraid or hungry, these sounds

parts.text: will always bring her to him.
parts.meaning: always make his mother come to him.

sentences.grammar: "His" is the young horse, "her" is the mother. The sounds are the doer here: they bring the mother.

sentences.context: "I reckon you're the smallest horse thieves I've ever come across," he said.
sentences.simple: He said: "I think you are the smallest horse thieves I have ever met."
sentences.main: I reckon you're the smallest horse thieves.

parts.meaning: I think
you are the smallest people who steal horses
that I have ever met,
he said.

sentences.grammar: "Reckon" = think (cowboy talk). "Come across" = meet by chance.

sentences.context: "How did you two brave, smart young'uns end up in Rattlesnake Flats?"
sentences.simple: "How did you two brave and clever kids get here to Rattlesnake Flats?"
sentences.main: How did you end up in Rattlesnake Flats?

parts.text: "How did you two brave, smart young'uns
parts.meaning: How did you two brave and clever kids
come to be in this town?

sentences.grammar: "Young'uns" = young ones, kids. "End up" = be somewhere in the end, without a plan.

sentences.context: Now that Slim could help Sunset, Jack wanted to look for the answer to the riddle.

sentences.main: Jack wanted to look for the answer.

parts.text: Now that Slim could help Sunset,
parts.meaning: Because Slim could help the colt now,

parts.text: Jack wanted to look for the answer to the riddle.
parts.meaning: Jack wanted to find the riddle's answer.

sentences.grammar: "Now that" means "because now".

sentences.context: "I wouldn't say 'yes' to many kids, Smiley, but you seem to have a knack with horses," said Slim.
sentences.simple: Slim said: "I don't let many children do this, Smiley, but you are good with horses."
sentences.main: You seem to have a knack with horses.

parts.meaning: I do not say yes to many children,
Annie,

parts.text: but you seem to have a knack with horses,"
parts.meaning: but you look like you are good with horses,
said Slim.

sentences.grammar: "But" shows the change: usually no, but for Annie yes. "A knack with" = a natural skill with.

sentences.context: Their way was lit by a nearly full moon and a million stars.
sentences.simple: The moon and lots of stars gave light to their path.
sentences.main: Their way was lit.

parts.meaning: Their path had light
from a moon that was almost round
and very many stars.

sentences.grammar: "Was lit by" tells you what made the light. "A million" here just means "very many".

sentences.context: He let go of the reins and tried to hold on to the saddle horn, but his weight pulled him down.
sentences.simple: He dropped the reins and tried to hold the front of the saddle. But he was too heavy, and he fell.
sentences.main: He let go and tried to hold on, but his weight pulled him down.

parts.text: He let go of the reins
parts.meaning: He stopped holding the reins

parts.text: and tried to hold on to the saddle horn,
parts.meaning: and tried to hold the high front part of the saddle,

parts.text: but his weight pulled him down.
parts.meaning: but his heavy body made him fall.

sentences.grammar: "But" shows that his try did not work.

sentences.context: Using all his strength, he pulled himself into the saddle.
sentences.simple: He used all his power and got up onto the saddle.
sentences.main: He pulled himself into the saddle.

parts.meaning: With all his power,

parts.text: he pulled himself into the saddle.
parts.meaning: he pulled his body up onto the horse's seat.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part at the start tells you how he did the main action.

sentences.context: Finally they came to a boxy open space surrounded by walls of rock and lit by moonlight.
sentences.simple: In the end they came to a square open place. It had rock walls all around and moonlight on it.
sentences.main: They came to a boxy open space.

parts.text: Finally they came to a boxy open space
parts.meaning: In the end they came to an open place shaped like a box
with rock walls all around it
and with light from the moon.

sentences.grammar: "Surrounded by ..." and "lit by ..." both tell you more about the open space.

sentences.context: If he hadn't come, I never would have gotten away!
sentences.simple: Without the ghost, I could not have escaped!
sentences.main: I never would have gotten away.

parts.meaning: If the ghost did not come,

parts.text: I never would have gotten away!
parts.meaning: I could not have escaped!

sentences.grammar: "If he hadn't ..., I would never have ..." talks about the past that did not happen. The ghost did come, so Jack did escape.

sentences.context: But folks say his ghost returns to the hotel piano to play ‘Red River Valley.’
sentences.simple: But people say his ghost comes back to the hotel piano and plays his song.
sentences.main: Folks say his ghost returns.

parts.meaning: But people say

parts.text: his ghost returns to the hotel piano
parts.meaning: his ghost comes back to the piano in the hotel
to play the song "Red River Valley".

sentences.grammar: "Folks" = people. "To play" tells you why the ghost comes back.

sentences.context: Since cowboys didn't mind, he didn't mind, either.
sentences.simple: Cowboys did not care about bad food, so Jack did not care either.
sentences.main: He didn't mind, either.

parts.meaning: Because cowboys were OK with it,
Jack was OK with it too.

sentences.grammar: "Since" here means "because". "Didn't mind" = was not unhappy about it. "Either" = "too" in a "not" sentence.

sentences.context: It's caused by sound bouncing off the canyon walls.
sentences.simple: It happens because the sound hits the rock walls and comes back.
sentences.main: It's caused by sound.

parts.meaning: It happens

parts.text: by sound bouncing off the canyon walls.
parts.meaning: because sound hits the canyon walls and comes back.

sentences.grammar: "Caused by" tells you the reason. "Bouncing off" = hitting something and coming back, like a ball.

sentences.context: "you might be short, but you're mighty tall in the brains."
sentences.simple: "You may be short, but you are very clever."
sentences.main: You might be short, but you're tall in the brains.

parts.meaning: you may be short,

parts.text: but you're mighty tall in the brains."
parts.meaning: but you are very clever.

sentences.grammar: "Mighty" = very (old cowboy talk). "Tall in the brains" is a joke: big in thinking.

sentences.context: "I'm grateful to you both for steering me straight," said Slim.
sentences.simple: Slim said: "Thank you both for helping me choose the right way."
sentences.main: I'm grateful to you both.

parts.meaning: I thank you two
because you helped me go the right way in life,
said Slim.

sentences.grammar: "Grateful to someone for something": the thing after "for" is the reason. "Steer" here means guide, like steering a horse.

sentences.context: WITH THANKS TO SMILEY AND SHORTY, TWO STRANGERS WHO CHANGED MY LIFE
sentences.simple: Thank you to Smiley and Shorty. I did not know them, but they changed my life.
sentences.main: With thanks to Smiley and Shorty.

parts.text: WITH THANKS TO SMILEY AND SHORTY,
parts.meaning: Thank you to Smiley and Shorty,
two people I did not know before
who made my life different.

sentences.grammar: A book dedication is often not a full sentence. "Who changed my life" tells you about the two strangers.

sentences.context: Then they ran all the way home, through the long shadows of the setting sun.
sentences.simple: Then they ran home through the long dark shapes made by the evening sun.
sentences.main: They ran all the way home.

parts.text: Then they ran all the way home,
parts.meaning: Then they ran the whole way to their house,

parts.text: through the long shadows of the setting sun.
parts.meaning: through long dark shapes on the ground, as the sun went down.

sentences.grammar: "All the way" = the whole way. The "setting sun" is the sun going down in the evening.
